claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase FCC equiatomic FeNiCrMn crystal with a random atomic distribution.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal contains thermal vacancies or pre-existing vacancy clusters.
Dislocations nucleate preferentially at vacancy clusters or surface defects.
Vacancy clusters and surface defects maximize local lattice distortion and act as stress concentrators.
Local stress concentration at vacancy clusters reduces the local unstable stacking-fault-energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Yield strength in FeNiCrMn is governed by unstable stacking-fault energy.
FeNiCrMn has high lattice distortion due to the presence of five elements, producing a fluctuating potential-energy landscape.
Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vector 1/6<112> create intrinsic stacking faults.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
The <11-1> orientation has a lower Schmid factor for the primary {111} slip system than <110>, so a higher applied stress is needed to reach the CRSS for partial emission.
The maximum yield stress for <11-1> will be approximately 15–20% higher than for <110>.
The sudden stress drop at yield corresponds to Shockley-partial emission and formation of intrinsic-stacking-fault ribbons.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults bounded by Shockley partials rather than a true HCP phase.
The HCP-like regions lack the long-range periodicity expected for a true HCP phase.
Yield strength is relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically with temperature because thermal activation facilitates dislocation glide.
A distinct HCP RDF peak near 2.5 Å, coordination number 12, specified bond angles, and a secondary yield plateau would diagnose a true phase transformation.
The magnitude of the orientation effect depends on the interatomic potential and initial vacancy concentration.

contradictions.description: FeNiCrMn is a four-element alloy, but the mechanism attributes its lattice distortion to five elements.

The hypothesis explains the higher <11-1> yield stress by saying this orientation maximizes resolved shear stress, whereas the mechanism says <11-1> has a lower Schmid factor and therefore develops less resolved shear stress at a given applied stress.
